The evidence in Source [S2] explicitly states: 'To further decrease the number of memory accesses during rendering, we split textures into density and appearance... components. This confirms that the split allows for deferred access (reading the appearance component only if necessary), which matches the claim.

It differs from CUDA-based accelerators like Instant-NGP by prioritizing browser portability and memory efficiency, achieving real-time frame rates on consumer hardware by combining coarse-to-fine grid queries with deferred appearance sampling [S2].

The evidence explicitly states that MERF is implemented as a Javascript 3D (three.js) web application orchestrated by a single GLSL fragment shader, which supports the claim of 'browser portability'. It contrasts this with Instant-NGP, which is 'implemented in CUDA and is therefore less portable across devices'. The evidence details the use of a 'multi-resolution hierarchy of occupancy grids' queried in a 'coarse-to-fine manner' and describes splitting textures to query density first and only read appearance if opacity is nonzero, which corresponds to 'deferred appearance sampling'. Finally, the evidence reports that on an RTX 3090, MERF renders at 'frame rates well above 100 FPS' while Instant-NGP achieves only 4 FPS, supporting the claim of achieving real-time frame rates on consumer hardware compared to Instant-NGP.
